newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGB futures end lower in thin trade.
newsitem.headline: JGB futures end lower in thin trade.

text.p: Key March Japanese government bond (JGB) futures ended Wednesday's Tokyo session lower in thin trade, following a rise in Tokyo stocks and the yen's fall against the dollar, traders said.
The March fell 0.16 to 126.17, after trading between 126.16 and 126.35. Turnover was 26,990 contracts.
"The March fell due to a firmer stock market and the dollar's rise above 124.00 yen," said a brokerage house trader.
The Nikkei average of 225 leading shares ended up 228.79 points, or 1.26 percent, at 18,409.96, after rising as high as 18,520.76.
Meanwhile, the dollar rose as high as 124.48 yen in the afternoon in Tokyo.
"Since the Ministry of Finance (MOF) voiced support for Japanese banks, worries about Japan's financial system have eased somewhat," said a trader at another brokerage house.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary committee on Monday that MOF will firmly support Japan's top 20 banks in their efforts to resolve their bad loan problems.
Worries about Japanese banks' problem loans had been a supportive factor for JGBs in recent weeks.
Traders said any downside for the March contract was expected to be limited due to short-covering pressure ahead of a shift in the benchmark status from March to June.
"The March is unlikely to fall below 126.00 due to short-covering pressure," the second trader said.
However, market participants' views about the timing of the benchmark shift were divided.
Most said it was likely to take place in the final week of February. Some, however, said it may take place as early as next week, while a few said it could be delayed until the first week of March.
Traders said the March contract's upside was likely to be limited at around 126.50, as profit-taking sales were expected to emerge near that level.
The yield of the benchmark cash 182nd JGB stood at 2.395 percent, up from 2.390 percent on Monday.
Japan's financial markets were closed on Tuesday for a national holiday.
The Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ) announced on Wednesday it would leave its long-term prime lending rate for February unchanged at a record low 2.5 percent.
